title: Image-sensor pinned well as capacitorless DRAM storage node
idea: Scarcity rule: no capacitor at all. Borrow the CMOS image sensor's pinned photodiode: a buried n-well under a p+ surface pin stores the bit as a few hundred electrons, and a transfer gate dumps it onto a floating diffusion read by a source-follower gain transistor (3T cell), so tiny charge still swings the bitline. The p+ pin keeps interface traps filled with holes, cutting generation leakage to a few electrons per second.
why: Removes the 60-75:1 capacitor pillar (fact 1) and its HAR/EUV steps (fact 4); pinned-well dark current implies seconds of retention vs 64 ms, cutting refresh energy (fact 3) ~10x, using image-sensor process steps U.S. fabs already run.

title: Solid-ionic double-layer nanocapacitor replaces the high-k pillar
idea: Scarcity rule: no high-k dielectric allowed. Store the bit in an electric double layer: a 3-5 nm solid ionic conductor (LiPON or a proton-conducting oxide) between ion-blocking electrodes gives Helmholtz capacitance of ~10-20 uF/cm2, about 10x a ZrO2 stack, so a planar or <=5:1 cup reaches 5 fF. Sub-redox voltages keep it purely capacitive (no faradaic reaction), so each write only displaces ions by a few angstroms.
why: Attacks the capacitor charge wall (fact 1): 10x areal capacitance turns a 70:1 pillar into a 5:1 cup, deleting the hardest etch and dielectric ALD steps; requires ion response under 10 ns at nm length scales.

title: Anodized-aluminum nanopores grow capacitor holes instead of etching them
idea: Scarcity rule: no high-aspect-ratio etch tool. Deposit an Al film over the cell transistors, imprint dimples at the storage-contact pitch, and anodize so self-ordered pores grow straight down at AR >150:1 by electrochemistry alone; ALD TiN/ZrO2/TiN lines the pores as cup capacitors after the pore-bottom barrier is thinned to open each contact.
why: Reaches the AR ~115 needed for more charge (fact 1) without HAR dry-etch tools and hardmask stacks, cutting capital intensity (fact 4); pore-to-contact registration is the main risk.

title: III-nitride resonant-tunneling floating well: ns write, hour retention
idea: Scarcity rule: refresh is banned. Store electrons in a GaN quantum well clad by AlN barriers (~2 eV offset) so thermionic leakage is negligible, and write through an AlN/GaN/AlN double-barrier resonant-tunneling stack that conducts only when the gate aligns its resonant level near 1 V. Read through the HEMT channel that the stored charge depletes.
why: Kills the leakage-tail refresh tax (fact 3: 16-33% idle power, 10-20% bandwidth); cold resonant tunneling avoids hot-carrier damage for DRAM-class endurance; moves the ULTRARAM idea to wide-gap GaN-on-Si.

title: Charge-density-wave electron-crystal bit in 1T-TaS2 nanoflakes
idea: Scarcity rule: no atom may move during a write. Store the bit as the electronic order of a 1T-TaS2 (or strain-stabilized analog) island: a ~ps current pulse switches the insulating commensurate CDW into a metallic hidden CDW state, a longer weak pulse restores it, and read uses the ~10x resistance contrast. Only the electron lattice rearranges, so there is no ionic fatigue.
why: Targets unlimited endurance with ps, fJ-class writes in a 2-terminal crosspoint element, sidestepping the CV2 floor (fact 10); room-temperature stability of the hidden state is the open physics question.

title: Sliding-ferroelectric van der Waals bilayer as fatigue-free gain gate
idea: Scarcity rule: no domain-wall pinning defects allowed. Use a sliding ferroelectric (rhombohedral bilayer MoS2 or parallel-stacked hBN), whose polarization flips by a one-third-lattice interlayer slip rather than ion displacement, as the gate of a 2D-channel read transistor; the dangling-bond-free vdW interface removes the charge trapping that limits HfO2 FeFETs.
why: 1T nondestructive-read cell with no capacitor (facts 1, 8) aiming for >1e15 cycles because sliding involves no oxygen-vacancy migration; needs wafer-scale aligned bilayers.

title: 2D interband tunnel-diode Goto pair: static bit with picoamp hold
idea: Scarcity rule: zero hold power and nothing above 1 V. Two series interband tunnel diodes (broken-gap black-phosphorus/SnSe2 vdW junctions with peak-to-valley ratio >100) form a bistable midpoint node held at valley current, and one access transistor reads and writes it like an SRAM half-cell.
why: Static storage removes refresh (fact 3) in 1T plus two stacked diodes (~8F2 vs 120-150F2 SRAM) and runs below 0.5 V, breaking the 1 V VARY floor (fact 10); valley current must fall below ~10 pA per cell.

title: VO2 hysteresis islands held bistable by chip waste heat
idea: Scarcity rule: no electrical hold power; the only free resource is the chip's own heat. W-doped VO2 islands are tuned so the die's ~65 C operating point sits inside their metal-insulator hysteresis loop; a Joule pulse sets an island metallic, a piezo-strain pulse (which shifts the transition temperature) resets it insulating, and read uses the ~100x resistance contrast.
why: Turns waste heat into retention power for a 2-terminal, refresh-free, sub-ns element (fact 3, no restore periphery fact 7); demands tight die-temperature control.

title: Endohedral ion-in-cage dipole: one molecule, one bit
idea: Scarcity rule: the bit gets one molecule of space. A metal ion inside an elongated fullerene or nitride-cluster cage (Li+@C70-type) sits in one of two off-center wells, a gate field flips it, and the dipole shifts the threshold of an underlying 2D transistor. No bond breaks, and the cage is chosen for a ~0.8 eV barrier giving ms-s retention.
why: Self-assembled monolayer density near 1 nm2 per bit bypasses the litho wall (fact 4) with attojoule writes and unbounded cycling; barrier engineering and single-molecule readout are speculative.

title: Contactless snap-through nanomembrane: bistable mechanical bit, vacuum-insulated
idea: Scarcity rule: vacuum is the only insulator allowed. A pre-buckled SiN or few-layer-graphene membrane over a sealed 20 nm cavity has two stable shapes; an electrostatic pulse from a bottom electrode snaps it up or down, and one access transistor senses the capacitance difference. It never touches anything, so there is no stiction or contact wear.
why: Zero leakage and zero hold power (fact 3) at GHz mechanical resonance for sub-100 nm membranes; elastic bending below 1% strain gives effectively unlimited cycles.

title: Nitrogen-cooled YBCO flux-loop memory with no helium
idea: Scarcity rule: no semiconductor in the cell and no helium (Qatar supply offline). Store the bit as a clockwise or counter-clockwise persistent current in a YBCO nanoloop at 77 K in liquid nitrogen; a current pulse through a phase-slip constriction writes it and a kinetic-inductance or nanoSQUID sensor reads it.
why: Zero static power and ps writes for LN2-immersed AI racks while avoiding the helium chokepoint; density is limited by loop inductance (~100 nm loops) and HTS junction yield.

title: Shallow-trap nitride liner turns the access transistor into the cell
idea: Scarcity rule: one transistor, no capacitor, no new material. Engineer the gate-stack SiN liner with shallow 0.6-0.8 eV traps that a 1.5 V pulse loads in ns by direct tunneling through 1.5 nm SiO2, shifting threshold for seconds; the shallow depth allows low-field cycling that avoids NAND-style oxide wear.
why: A ~4F2 1T cell from standard materials removes the capacitor (facts 1, 2) and its EUV layers (fact 4) while seconds of retention cut refresh; 1e15-cycle endurance is the risk.

title: Coulomb-blockade nanodot bit: ten electrons, held by charging energy
idea: Scarcity rule: the bit gets 1000x less charge. Self-assembled 2 nm Si dots in the gate oxide store 5-10 electrons each, and their Coulomb charging energy (>10 kT) blocks back-tunneling so retention comes from electrostatics rather than oxide thickness; a sensitive gain transistor reads the threshold shift.
why: Shrinks stored charge from ~30,000 to ~10 electrons, deleting the capacitor (fact 1) and cutting write energy ~1000x (fact 10); room-temperature blockade needs tight dot uniformity.

title: Freestanding epitaxial SrTiO3 membranes transferred as k-300 capacitor dielectric
idea: Scarcity rule: no dielectric with k below 100. Grow single-crystal SrTiO3/BaSrTiO3 on a water-soluble Sr3Al2O6 sacrificial layer, release wafer-scale membranes, and bond them onto the DRAM transistor array below 400 C; the dead-layer-free crystal keeps k ~300 at 10 nm so planar or 3:1 caps reach 5 fF.
why: Beats the k ~70 target (fact 1) 4x over, collapsing capacitor height and its HAR/EUV steps (fact 4); wafer-scale transfer and electrode interfaces are the risks.

title: Negative-capacitance HZO layer amplifies cap density in series
idea: Scarcity rule: stay inside today's capacitor footprint, no taller pillar. Add a thin HZO layer in series with the ZrO2, matched so the HZO is stabilized on its negative-capacitance branch; the series stack's capacitance then exceeds ZrO2 alone, raising stored charge 1.5-3x at the same aspect ratio.
why: Raises Cs from ~5 to 8-15 fF without AR 115 (fact 1), or drops AR to ~40:1; must stay non-hysteretic at ns speeds.

title: SiGe quantum-well hole pocket extends floating-body retention
idea: Scarcity rule: silicon-family materials only, no capacitor. Grow a buried Si0.6Ge0.4 well in the body of a vertical gate-all-around channel; its ~200 meV valence-band offset traps holes written by impact ionization or GIDL and shifts threshold for read, while the offset blocks hole recombination into source and drain.
why: Capacitorless 4F2 vertical cell (facts 1, 2, 4) with ~100x longer retention than plain floating-body cells via band confinement; SiGe epitaxy is mature in U.S. fabs.

title: Altermagnet tunnel junction: magnetoresistance without stray fields
idea: Scarcity rule: no net magnetization allowed, since stray fields set MRAM pitch. Store the bit in the Neel vector of an altermagnet (RuO2, MnTe or Mn5Si3) whose spin-split bands still give tunneling magnetoresistance, and flip it with spin-splitter or spin-orbit torque at THz-class dynamics.
why: 10 nm-pitch magnetic bits with no dipolar crosstalk, ps writes and unlimited endurance (density and energy axes); room-temperature TMR magnitude is unproven.

title: Capacitive-read crosspoint: hysteretic MFS stack, no access transistor
idea: Scarcity rule: no transistor at the cell. Each crosspoint is a metal/ferroelectric/semiconductor stack whose polarization leaves the semiconductor in accumulation or depletion, and a sub-coercive AC read pulse senses the 3-5x small-signal capacitance difference, drawing no DC sneak current and never disturbing the state. Only writes switch polarization.
why: Stackable 4F2 crosspoint without selectors (facts 2, 4, 7) with nondestructive read removing restore (fact 8); ferroelectric write endurance (~1e11) needs write-sparing.

title: Conducting domain-wall bit in thin lithium niobate mesas
idea: Scarcity rule: the sense path may use no stored charge at all. A 10 nm LiNbO3 mesa either contains or lacks a charged conducting domain wall bridging two side electrodes; an in-plane voltage pulse injects or erases the wall, and read is its nA-level current, a nondestructive resistive read.
why: 2-terminal, ns-write, nondestructive read (fact 8) at low voltage on a thin-film LiNbO3 platform growing for photonics; endurance and sub-20 nm scaling are unproven.

title: Self-selective optical global refresh through a transparent top plate
idea: Scarcity rule: zero refresh bandwidth. A transparent ITO cell plate lets a chip-wide LED flash generate carriers in a photodiode junction at each storage node, and the node's own voltage steers the photocurrent so '1' nodes recharge toward VARY while '0' nodes drain to ground, refreshing every cell in parallel with no row cycling.
why: Removes the 10-20% refresh bandwidth loss and per-row activation energy (fact 3) and refresh-driven activations (fact 9); steering selectivity and optical access through BEOL are the risks.

title: Magnetoelectric BiFeO3 voltage-written magnet with TMR read
idea: Scarcity rule: no current may cross any insulator during a write. Ferroelectric switching of a BiFeO3 layer rotates its antiferromagnetic order, which exchange-couples to the CoFe free layer of an MTJ, so a ~100 mV gate pulse writes and TMR reads; charge only moves capacitively.
why: Attojoule-class nonvolatile writes (facts 3, 10) with no barrier stress; BiFeO3 fatigue and switching speed must reach 1e15 cycles and ns.

title: CCD-loop memory: charge packets circulate, no per-bit contact
idea: Scarcity rule: no transistor or contact per bit. Bits ride as charge packets in buried-channel CCD loops of 64 cells clocked by 2-phase gates, and one sense-and-regenerate stage per loop reads and restores each packet as it passes, so a bit costs only ~2F2 of gate pitch.
why: Removes per-bit transistors and contacts (fact 4) for ~3x density at the same F; buried-channel dark current gives seconds of retention; the ~32-clock average wait adds latency.

title: Avalanche-gain readout lets a 50-electron node hold a bit
idea: Scarcity rule: storage charge is cut 300x. Each storage node sits on a junction biased just below breakdown, and during read a stored packet of ~50 electrons triggers a quenched SPAD-style avalanche with ~1e5 charge gain while an empty node stays silent, so a 0.01 fF planar node suffices.
why: Deletes the capacitor charge wall (fact 1) entirely with fJ-scale reads; dark counts and afterpulsing set the raw BER that ECC must absorb.

title: Gallium-oxide access transistor plus refresh-rate register cuts refresh 4x
idea: Forced limit (DDR/HBM interface unchanged): keep the pins and protocol, and change only what the die reports. Replace the Si access transistor with a 4.8 eV beta-Ga2O3 vertical channel whose off current is ~1e-6 of Si so 5 fF holds for minutes, and have the die permanently report the slowest refresh-rate code already defined in the MR4 temperature/refresh register, so unmodified controllers issue 4x fewer REFs.
why: Uses an existing spec field to monetize retention: refresh energy and bandwidth (fact 3) down ~75% with zero controller change; Ga2O3 crystal quality at BEOL thermal budget is the risk.

title: Tri-level cells pack 24 Gb into a 16 Gb array
idea: Forced limit (DDR/HBM interface unchanged): only densities JEDEC already defines may ship. Store three charge levels per cell and encode 3 bits in every 2 cells (9 states >= 8) with a two-step sense against half-level reference cells inside tRCD, so a 16 Gb-sized array ships as a standard, already-legal 24 Gb DDR5 die.
why: +50% bits per wafer with no interface change, worth about three node shrinks of cost per bit (fact 4); halved sense margin must be bought back with a higher-Cs dielectric.

title: Antiferroelectric transition boosts stored charge in standard 1T1C
idea: Forced limit (DDR/HBM interface unchanged): same 1T1C array, sense amps and timings. Replace the ZrO2 dielectric with a tuned antiferroelectric ZrO2/HfZrO film and bias the plate so the 0-to-VARY swing crosses the field-induced AFE-to-FE transition, whose extra polarization charge gives an effective k above 100; the film relaxes back on discharge with no remanence or wake-up.
why: 2-3x Cs at the same AR (fact 1), or today's Cs at ~30:1; reversible AFE transitions avoid domain pinning, targeting >1e15 cycles with unchanged timings.

title: Low-barrier volatile MTJ refreshed by the REF commands DDR already sends
idea: Forced limit (DDR/HBM interface unchanged): DDR insists on refresh, so make refresh useful. Use a 12-15 nm STT-MTJ designed with low thermal stability (Delta ~25-30, retention of seconds), which cuts write current ~4x so a tiny access transistor suffices, and let standard REF commands trigger internal read-and-rewrite of aging rows; holding costs zero leakage.
why: MRAM-style 1T1R density with DRAM refresh semantics, ~50 fJ writes and no capacitor (facts 1, 2); low current density extends barrier life, but retention spread and write-error rate are risks.

title: VCMA precessional MTJ write with retry loop hidden inside tWR
idea: Forced limit (DDR/HBM interface unchanged): every write must finish inside DDR5's ~30 ns tWR. A voltage-controlled-magnetic-anisotropy MTJ switches by a 0.5 ns precessional pulse at ~0.5 V with near-zero current, and because its single-shot error rate is ~1e-3, the die runs write-verify-retry up to 10 times within tWR, turning a probabilistic element into a deterministic DDR write.
why: Fixed spec slack becomes the reliability budget: fJ nonvolatile writes (facts 3, 10) with negligible barrier current, so endurance is effectively unlimited.

title: Racetrack rows: ACT shifts a domain-wall track, tRCD hides it
idea: Forced limit (DDR/HBM interface unchanged): keep DDR's ACT-then-READ page model. Map each row address to a shift position of perpendicular domain-wall racetracks under a line of read/write heads; ACT drives a current pulse that moves the tracks to that position within tRCD (~14 ns at ~500 m/s covers ~64 bits at 100 nm spacing), the heads latch the row into sense amps, and PRE writes it back.
why: One head per 64 bits instead of a transistor per bit gives ~10x cell-area density (facts 4, 7), magnetic storage needs no refresh and has no wear; domain-wall pinning variability sets the risk.

title: Bank-wide floating-body refresh fired in a single REF slot
idea: Forced limit (DDR/HBM interface unchanged): REF commands keep arriving on the spec schedule. Use bistable floating-body cells whose parasitic bipolar transistor latches, so one REF fires a bank-wide source pulse that pumps '1' cells back to full hole charge by impact ionization while '0' cells stay empty, restoring every row at once; the remaining REFs become no-ops.
why: Cuts refresh energy (46 fJ/bit, fact 3) and refresh activations (fact 9) ~1000x via parallel restore in a capacitorless 4F2 cell; bipolar latch margin across temperature is the risk.

title: Planar 1.5 fF capacitor rescued by stronger invisible on-die ECC
idea: Forced limit (DDR/HBM interface unchanged): the host must see ordinary DDR5 data. Shrink the capacitor to a low-AR 1.5 fF cup that tolerates raw BER near 1e-5, and replace DDR5's internal SEC(136,128) with a hidden double-error-correcting code over 256-bit internal words (same ~6% parity) plus offset-cancelled sensing inside tRCD.
why: Spends invisible ECC and sense-time slack to delete the 60-75:1 pillar (fact 1) and several HAR/EUV steps (fact 4), ~20% lower wafer cost; partial-write read-modify-write must fit in tWR.

title: Dual-mode HZO capacitor snapshots to polarization on self-refresh entry
idea: Forced limit (DDR/HBM interface unchanged): power states are only those DDR defines. Run an HZO capacitor below its coercive field as a plain DRAM capacitor in normal operation; on Self-Refresh Entry the die sweeps rows above coercive field to store data as polarization and powers the array off, and after Self-Refresh Exit each row's first ACT performs the destructive ferroelectric read and restores it as charge within tRCD.
why: Self-refresh power falls to ~0 (fact 3: refresh is 16-33% of idle power) while ferroelectric switching happens only per power-down, so ~1e11 FE endurance is ample; lazy restore fits within tXS.

title: HBM-pin-compatible core dies built in U.S. logic fabs with deep-trench cells
idea: Forced limit (DDR/HBM interface unchanged): drop into existing HBM3E stacks and controllers. Fabricate core dies in U.S. logic foundries on their deep-trench eDRAM process (bulk-Si trench caps of ~30-40 fF), stack them on a standard HBM base die, and sell them as lower-density but available HBM for inference tiers.
why: U.S. manufacturability and capital (fact 4; U.S. makes 1-2% of DRAM): reuses depreciated logic capacity with no new DRAM fab; ~1/3 DRAM density but viable at 4x prices.

title: Hybrid gain cell: silicon read transistor, WSe2 write transistor
idea: Forced limit (DDR/HBM interface unchanged): ACT/RD/WR/PRE behavior unchanged. A 2T gain cell stores the bit on the gate of a Si FinFET read device, written through a BEOL monolayer WSe2 p-FET whose 1.6 eV gap and atomically thin body give off current below 1e-19 A; reads are nondestructive, so the die skips restore inside tRAS and uses the slack to precharge early.
why: No capacitor (facts 1, 2), minutes of retention (fact 3), and no restore energy for the 128x overfetched page (fact 8); 2D transfer yield is the risk.

title: Crested-barrier floating node written by DRAM's existing 3 V wordline rail
idea: Forced limit (DDR/HBM interface unchanged): no new supply pins, so reuse the ~3 V VPP rail DRAM already has. Store charge on a floating node behind a crested SiO2/Si3N4/SiO2 barrier whose peaked profile collapses under high field for ns writes but stays thick at hold fields for hours of retention; reads sense the storage transistor's threshold shift.
why: The existing wordline rail powers a quasi-nonvolatile 1T cell with no capacitor (facts 1, 3); endurance under repeated tunneling writes is the unknown.

title: Significance-aware HBM lanes: compact cells for bf16 mantissa bits
idea: Forced limit (DDR/HBM interface unchanged): DQ lanes and bursts stay identical. Because inference stacks lay out bf16/fp8 tensors with fixed bit positions per DQ lane, build core dies whose arrays behind sign/exponent lanes keep full-size capacitors while arrays behind low-mantissa lanes use half-height capacitors with relaxed retention (raw BER ~1e-4), enabled by an existing mode-register write and defaulting to full reliability.
why: ~25-35% less capacitor height/area per stack for AI inference where LSB errors are tolerable (density, cost per bit) with an identical interface; depends on controller address and lane mapping.

title: Backside deep-trench storage capacitors under a frontside transistor array
idea: Forced limit (DDR/HBM interface unchanged): same die footprint and pinout. After frontside transistors and periphery are built and bonded to a carrier, thin the wafer and etch storage trenches into crystalline Si from the backside (Bosch/cryo Si etch reaches 100:1), contacting each access transistor drain through the thinned body, which frees the frontside for periphery and bitline routing.
why: AR >100 in silicon (fact 1) decoupled from the transistor stack, with periphery congestion relieved (fact 7); reuses backside-power-delivery process know-how.

title: Buried-oxide-isolated storage nodes immune to row hammer coupling
idea: Forced limit (DDR/HBM interface unchanged): controllers keep sending the same RFM and refresh, so the cell itself must stop flipping. Isolate each storage-node junction from the shared substrate with a local buried-oxide pocket (selective SiGe removal and oxidation) and shield it with a grounded buried plate between adjacent wordlines, cutting the electron-injection and trap-assisted paths that aggressor activations exploit.
why: Raises the row-hammer threshold from ~1k to >100k activations (fact 9), removing mitigation overhead, and trims the junction-leakage tail (fact 3).

title: Tunnel-FET access device eliminates the thermionic leakage tail
idea: Forced limit (DDR/HBM interface unchanged): same timings, so the write must still finish within tWR. Replace the access MOSFET with a vertical SiGe/Si tunnel FET whose off state relies on band misalignment rather than a thermionic barrier, so subthreshold leakage drops below 0.01 fA and barely changes with temperature, while its lower on-current still charges 5 fF within tWR.
why: Removes the leakage tail (fact 3) and the 2x hot-temperature refresh penalty, reported via the existing refresh-rate register; on-current and ambipolar leakage are the risks.

title: Coaxial dual-node pillar stores two bits in one capacitor footprint
idea: Forced limit (DDR/HBM interface unchanged): pitch and interface stay, so get more bits per pillar. Build each pillar as three concentric shells (an inner storage electrode, a shared grounded middle plate with dielectric on both faces, and an outer annular storage electrode), each storage electrode tied to its own vertical access transistor, so one footprint holds two independent ~4 fF bits.
why: Doubles capacitor area used per footprint (fact 1) with 4F2 vertical transistors underneath, ~1.5x density at the same litho (fact 4); concentric deposition in HAR holes is the risk.

title: Self-healing clearing electrodes burn out capacitor weak spots at test
idea: Forced limit (DDR/HBM interface unchanged): the die must look like normal DDR5, so fix the leakage tail inside the cell. Make the capacitor top electrode an ultrathin clearable layer, as in metallized-film capacitors: a wafer-sort overvoltage pulse makes each dielectric weak spot conduct and locally oxidizes or vaporizes the electrode around it, isolating the defect so the dielectric can be thinned ~20%.
why: ~20% more Cs from a thinner dielectric (fact 1) and a tighter retention tail (fact 3) with no interface change; each cleared area must stay below ~5% of the electrode.

title: Charge-plasma junctionless storage node kills GIDL leakage tail
idea: Forced limit (DDR/HBM interface unchanged): unchanged timings and voltages. Remove the doped n+ storage-node junction: the access channel is undoped and the storage-node extension is electrostatically doped by a low-work-function metal (charge plasma), so no metallurgical pn junction remains for junction leakage or GIDL band-to-band tunneling.
why: Shrinks the <=13 fA leakage tail (fact 3) ~10x, stretching retention and cutting refresh via the existing refresh-rate register, while removing implant and anneal steps.

title: JEDEC cell-agnostic conformance badge for non-capacitor DDR5 dies
idea: Forced limit (DDR/HBM interface unchanged) turned into policy: fund a JEDEC/CHIPS conformance suite that certifies any DDR5/HBM3 die by behavior alone (timings, refresh tolerance, 1e16-write endurance stress, hammer tests) rather than by cell type, and pair it with federal procurement preference for certified second-source dies built on new storage elements.
why: Cuts the adoption barrier for new storage elements to zero controller changes and shortens qualification by years, widening supply and U.S. manufacturability.

title: Sell retention-fallout dies as permanent fast-refresh DDR5 SKUs
idea: Forced limit (DDR/HBM interface unchanged): standard controllers only. Dies that miss 64 ms retention because of a weak-cell tail are fused to always report the hot-temperature refresh-rate code (2x or 4x refresh) in the existing MR4 register, so stock controllers refresh them faster, and they sell at a discount into capacity-hungry, bandwidth-tolerant tiers such as CXL expanders and inference KV-cache.
why: Recovers a few percent of wafer output now scrapped or downbinned, raising usable bit supply immediately with zero capex (cost per bit, supply).

title: Nitrogen-immersed DDR5 DIMMs with sub-femtofarad cryo-optimized cells
idea: Forced limit (DDR/HBM interface unchanged): same DDR5 edge connector and protocol, so move the whole DIMM into the LN2 or cold-plate loop of an AI rack. At 77 K access leakage falls >1e6, so a redesigned array uses ~1 fF planar capacitors with half-length bitlines to keep Cs/Cbl and holds data for hours, while the PHY is retuned for 77 K thresholds but signals per spec.
why: Removes the HAR capacitor (fact 1) and refresh (fact 3), and higher mobility allows lower voltages (fact 10); nitrogen is abundant (no helium), cooling energy is the tradeoff.

title: Hammer-triggered twin-cell mode doubles signal only where needed
idea: Forced limit (DDR/HBM interface unchanged): the controller only issues ACT/REF/RFM as today. When the die's internal activation counter flags a row as an aggressor or victim, it silently remaps that row into twin-cell mode, storing each bit as a charge and its complement in two adjacent cells sensed differentially, which doubles signal and makes single-cell disturb flips harmless.
why: Neutralizes row hammer (fact 9) and weak-cell tails (fact 3) without host mitigation, and allows thinner cells elsewhere; spare rows absorb the small capacity cost.
